notes.front: What is a scaffold, in Subpart L?
notes.back: Any temporary elevated platform, supported or suspended, and its supporting structure, including anchorage points, used to support employees, materials or both.
notes.explanation: The definition covers both supported and suspended platforms, and counts anchorage points as part of the scaffold.
notes.example: Like the stack of frames and planks along a house front for rendering, or a cradle hung from a roof for window work.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.450(b), p. 252
notes.evidence: Scaffold means any temporary elevated platform (supported or suspended) and its supporting structure (including points of anchorage), used for supporting employees or materials or both.

notes.front: What is an aerial lift, under section 1926.453?
notes.back: A vehicle-mounted device to raise personnel to job-sites above ground, such as extensible or articulating boom platforms, aerial ladders and vertical towers.
notes.explanation: Section 1926.451’s general scaffold rules do not apply to aerial lifts; section 1926.453 alone covers them.
notes.example: Like the “cherry picker” basket on a lorry that lifts a worker to a street light.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.453(a)(2), p. 270
notes.evidence: Aerial lifts include the following types of vehicle-mounted aerial devices used to elevate personnel to job-sites above ground: (i) Extensible boom platforms; (ii) Aerial ladders; (iii) Articulating boom platforms; (iv) Vertical towers

notes.front: Who must design a scaffold?
notes.back: A qualified person; the scaffold is then built and loaded according to that design.
notes.explanation: Appendix A to Subpart L gives non-mandatory examples of criteria that meet the capacity rules.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(a)(6), p. 253
notes.evidence: Scaffolds shall be designed by a qualified person and shall be constructed and loaded in accordance with that design.

notes.front: What load limit applies when using a scaffold?
notes.back: Neither the scaffold nor its components may be loaded beyond their maximum intended loads or rated capacities, whichever is less.
notes.explanation: The lower of the two figures is the one that governs.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(f)(1), p. 259
notes.evidence: Scaffolds and scaffold components shall not be loaded in excess of their maximum intended loads or rated capacities, whichever is less.

notes.front: How must each platform on a scaffold’s working levels be planked?
notes.back: Fully planked or decked between the front uprights and guardrail supports, with gaps between units and uprights of no more than 1 inch.
notes.explanation: A wider space is allowed only where the employer shows it is necessary, such as fitting round uprights.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(b)(1)(i), p. 253
notes.evidence: shall be installed so that the space between adjacent units and the space between the platform and the uprights is no more than 1 inch (2.5 cm) wide

notes.front: What is the minimum width of a scaffold platform or walkway, as a general rule?
notes.back: 18 inches.
notes.explanation: Some types, such as ladder jack and pump jack scaffolds, may be 12 inches, and boatswains’ chairs have no minimum.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(b)(2), p. 253
notes.evidence: each scaffold platform and walkway shall be at least 18 inches (46 cm) wide

notes.front: How far from the face of the work may a scaffold platform’s front edge be, as a rule?
notes.back: No more than 14 inches, unless guardrails or personal fall arrest systems protect that edge.
notes.explanation: Outrigger scaffolds are limited to 3 inches and plastering and lathing to 18 inches.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(b)(3), p. 254
notes.evidence: the front edge of all platforms shall not be more than 14 inches (36 cm) from the face of the work, unless guardrail systems are erected along the front edge and/or personal fall arrest systems are used

notes.front: How far must each end of an unrestrained scaffold platform extend over the centreline of its support?
notes.back: At least 6 inches, unless it is cleated or otherwise restrained by hooks or equivalent means.
notes.explanation: A platform 10 feet or less long must not overhang its support by more than 12 inches, with stated exceptions.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(b)(4), p. 254
notes.evidence: unless cleated or otherwise restrained by hooks or equivalent means, shall extend over the centerline of its support at least 6 inches (15 cm)

notes.front: On what must the poles, legs, posts, frames and uprights of a supported scaffold bear?
notes.back: Base plates and mud sills or other adequate firm foundation.
notes.explanation: Footings must be level, sound, rigid and able to carry the loaded scaffold without settling or displacement.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(c)(2), p. 255
notes.evidence: bear on base plates and mud sills or other adequate firm foundation. (i) Footings shall be level, sound, rigid, and capable of supporting the loaded scaffold without settling or displacement.

notes.front: May unstable objects be used to support a scaffold or as a working platform?
notes.back: No, for both purposes.
notes.explanation: Front-end loaders and similar equipment may support platforms only if the manufacturer designed them for it.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(c)(2)(ii)–(iii), p. 255
notes.evidence: Unstable objects shall not be used to support scaffolds or platform units. (iii) Unstable objects shall not be used as working platforms.

notes.front: When must a supported scaffold be restrained from tipping by guying, tying or bracing?
notes.back: When its height to base width ratio, including outriggers, is more than four to one.
notes.explanation: Guys, ties and braces go where horizontal members support both inner and outer legs.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(c)(1), p. 254
notes.evidence: Supported scaffolds with a height to base width (including outrigger supports, if used) ratio of more than four to one (4:1) shall be restrained from tipping by guying, tying, bracing, or equivalent means

notes.front: When must a proper means of access, such as a ladder or stair tower, be provided to a scaffold platform?
notes.back: When the platform is more than 2 feet above or below a point of access.
notes.explanation: The listed means include portable, hook-on and attachable ladders, stair towers, ramps and walkways.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(e)(1), p. 257
notes.evidence: When scaffold platforms are more than 2 feet (0.6 m) above or below a point of access

notes.front: When must a competent person inspect scaffolds and components for visible defects?
notes.back: Before each work shift, and after any occurrence that could affect structural integrity.
notes.explanation: Both the start of each shift and any event that could affect integrity trigger an inspection.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(f)(3), p. 259
notes.evidence: Scaffolds and scaffold components shall be inspected for visible defects by a competent person before each work shift, and after any occurrence which could affect a scaffold’s structural integrity.

notes.front: Which two kinds of scaffold does Subpart L prohibit outright?
notes.back: Shore scaffolds and lean-to scaffolds.
notes.explanation: Their use is prohibited in the rules on using scaffolds.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(f)(2), p. 259
notes.evidence: The use of shore or lean-to scaffolds is prohibited.

notes.front: Under whose supervision may scaffolds be erected, moved, dismantled or altered?
notes.back: A competent person qualified in that work; experienced, trained employees selected by that person do it.
notes.explanation: Section 1926.451(f)(7) joins the competent person’s supervision to a choice of crew.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(f)(7), p. 259
notes.evidence: Scaffolds shall be erected, moved, dismantled, or altered only under the supervision and direction of a competent person qualified in scaffold erection, moving, dismantling or alteration.

notes.front: What are the minimum clearances between a scaffold and insulated power lines below 300 volts, and from 300 volts to 50 kV?
notes.back: 3 feet below 300 volts; 10 feet from 300 volts to 50 kV.
notes.explanation: Uninsulated lines under 50 kV also need 10 feet; above 50 kV either kind needs 10 feet plus 0.4 inches per kV over 50, or twice the insulator length, never under 10 feet.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(f)(6), p. 259
notes.evidence: 3 feet (0.9 m). 10 feet (3.1m). 10 feet (3.1 m) plus 0.4 inches (1.0 cm) for each 1 kv over 50 kv.

notes.front: When may employees work on or from scaffolds during storms or high winds?
notes.back: Only if a competent person decides it is safe and they are protected by a personal fall arrest system or wind screens.
notes.explanation: Wind screens may be used only if the scaffold is secured against the expected wind forces.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(f)(12), p. 260
notes.evidence: is prohibited during storms or high winds unless a competent person has determined that it is safe for employees to be on the scaffold and those employees are protected by a personal fall arrest system or wind screens

notes.front: May boxes or barrels be placed on a scaffold platform to raise the working height?
notes.back: No. Makeshift devices such as boxes and barrels must not be used for that.
notes.explanation: Ladders may not be used to raise the working height either, except on large area scaffolds meeting set criteria.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(f)(14), p. 260
notes.evidence: Makeshift devices, such as but not limited to boxes and barrels, shall not be used on top of scaffold platforms to increase the working level height of employees.

notes.front: Above what height must each employee on a scaffold be protected from falling to a lower level?
notes.back: More than 10 feet above the lower level.
notes.explanation: The type of protection depends on the scaffold type, as Subpart L sets out.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(g)(1), p. 260
notes.evidence: Each employee on a scaffold more than 10 feet (3.1 m) above a lower level shall be protected from falling to that lower level.

notes.front: What fall protection is required on a single-point or two-point adjustable suspension scaffold?
notes.back: Both a personal fall arrest system and a guardrail system.
notes.explanation: Crawling boards, by contrast, allow a personal fall arrest system or a guardrail system, among other options.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(g)(1)(ii), p. 260
notes.evidence: Each employee on a single-point or two-point adjustable suspension scaffold shall be protected by both a personal fall arrest system and guardrail system

notes.front: For supported scaffolds placed in service after 1 January 2000, where must the toprail’s top edge be?
notes.back: Between 38 and 45 inches above the platform surface.
notes.explanation: Guardrails must be on all open sides and ends before the scaffold is released for use by anyone other than the erection crew.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(g)(4)(ii), p. 261
notes.evidence: shall be installed between 38 inches (0.97 m) and 45 inches (1.2 m) above the platform surface

notes.front: Who decides whether fall protection is feasible and safe for employees erecting or dismantling supported scaffolds?
notes.back: A competent person, designated by the employer.
notes.explanation: Protection must be provided where it is feasible and does not create a greater hazard.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(g)(2), p. 261
notes.evidence: the employer shall have a competent person determine the feasibility and safety of providing fall protection for employees erecting or dismantling supported scaffolds

notes.front: Who must train each employee who works while on a scaffold?
notes.back: A person qualified in the subject matter.
notes.explanation: The training covers recognising the scaffold’s hazards and the procedures to control or minimise them.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.454(a), p. 271
notes.evidence: The employer shall have each employee who performs work while on a scaffold trained by a person qualified in the subject matter

notes.front: What are two areas scaffold user training must include, as applicable?
notes.back: Any two of, among others: electrical, fall and falling object hazards; proper use of the scaffold and handling of materials; the maximum intended load.
notes.explanation: Section 1926.454(a) lists five areas.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.454(a)(1), p. 271
notes.evidence: The nature of any electrical hazards, fall hazards and falling object hazards in the work area

notes.front: What fall restraint does section 1926.453 require when working from an aerial lift?
notes.back: A body belt worn with a lanyard attached to the boom or basket; belting off to an adjacent pole or structure is not permitted.
notes.explanation: A note adds that body belts are acceptable in a restraint or tethering system but not in a personal fall arrest system.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.453(b)(2)(v), p. 270
notes.evidence: A body belt shall be worn and a lanyard attached to the boom or basket when working from an aerial lift.

notes.front: How often must the controls of a boom platform aerial lift be tested?
notes.back: Each day before use.
notes.explanation: Only authorised persons may operate an aerial lift.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.453(b)(2)(i), p. 270
notes.evidence: Lift controls shall be tested each day prior to use to determine that such controls are in safe working condition.

notes.front: A scaffold is intended to carry at most 1,000 pounds of workers and materials. What must it support without failure, besides its own weight?
notes.back: A: 4,000 pounds.
notes.choices:
A) 4,000 pounds
B) 2,000 pounds
C) 1,000 pounds
D) 6,000 pounds
notes.choicesExplained: C gives no margin. B is half the required factor. D is the factor for suspension ropes, not the scaffold itself.
notes.explanation: Four times the maximum intended load of 1,000 pounds is 4,000 pounds.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(a)(1), p. 253
notes.evidence: its own weight and at least 4 times the maximum intended load applied or transmitted to it

notes.front: A frame scaffold’s working platform is one 12-inch plank with a 4-inch gap beside it. Nothing makes the area narrow. What is wrong?
notes.back: C: it must be fully planked, at least 18 inches wide, with gaps no more than 1 inch.
notes.choices:
A) Only the gap
B) Nothing
C) It must be fully planked, at least 18 inches wide, with gaps no more than 1 inch
D) Only the width
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores both breaches. A and D each miss one of the two.
notes.explanation: The 12-inch minimum applies only to listed types such as ladder jack and pump jack scaffolds.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(b)(1), p. 253
notes.evidence: Each platform on all working levels of scaffolds shall be fully planked or decked between the front uprights and the guardrail supports

notes.front: A crew sets a frame scaffold’s legs on stacks of loose hollow blocks on soft ground. What does Subpart L require instead?
notes.back: C: base plates and mud sills or other firm foundation.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, if the blocks are level
B) Wider blocks
C) Base plates and mud sills or other firm foundation
D) A daily check only
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D keep unstable objects as supports, which Subpart L forbids.
notes.explanation: Footings must carry the loaded scaffold without settling or displacement.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(c)(2)(ii), p. 255
notes.evidence: Unstable objects shall not be used to support scaffolds or platform units.

notes.front: Workers climb the crossbraces of a frame scaffold to reach a platform 7 feet above the ground. What should they use instead?
notes.back: D: a proper means such as a ladder, stair tower or ramp.
notes.choices:
A) The crossbraces, if they are careful
B) A rope
C) Nothing; access rules start at 10 feet
D) A proper means such as a ladder, stair tower or ramp
notes.choicesExplained: A: crossbraces may never be used for access. B is not a listed means. C: the access rule starts at more than 2 feet.
notes.explanation: The platform is more than 2 feet above the point of access.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(e)(1), p. 257
notes.evidence: Crossbraces shall not be used as a means of access.

notes.front: Overnight a delivery truck clips a scaffold. The morning shift is about to climb it. What must happen first?
notes.back: D: a competent person inspects it for defects.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing unless there is visible collapse
B) Work starts; inspections are weekly
C) The workers look it over themselves
D) A competent person inspects it for defects
notes.choicesExplained: B: inspections are before each shift. C: the inspector must be a competent person. A: any occurrence that could affect structural integrity triggers an inspection.
notes.explanation: Both the new shift and the impact call for inspection.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(f)(3), p. 259
notes.evidence: shall be inspected for visible defects by a competent person before each work shift, and after any occurrence which could affect a scaffold’s structural integrity

notes.front: A scaffold must go up beside an insulated 13 kV line. What is the least clearance allowed?
notes.back: D: 10 feet.
notes.choices:
A) 3 feet
B) 6 feet
C) 20 feet
D) 10 feet
notes.choicesExplained: A applies only below 300 volts. B is not a figure in the table. C is more than the table requires.
notes.explanation: 13 kV falls in the 300 volts to 50 kV band.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(f)(6), p. 259
notes.evidence: Scaffolds shall not be erected, used, dismantled, altered, or moved such that they or any conductive material handled on them might come closer to exposed and energized power lines than as follows

notes.front: A painter works on a supported scaffold platform 8 feet above the ground. Does Subpart L require fall protection for him?
notes.back: A: no, the scaffold trigger is more than 10 feet.
notes.choices:
A) No, the scaffold trigger is more than 10 feet
B) Yes, above 6 feet
C) Yes, always
D) Only if he uses a ladder
notes.choicesExplained: B is the Subpart M trigger for other surfaces. C and D have no basis in the scaffold rule.
notes.explanation: Other rules, such as the 14-inch front-edge limit, still apply below 10 feet.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(g)(1), p. 260
notes.evidence: Each employee on a scaffold more than 10 feet (3.1 m) above a lower level shall be protected from falling to that lower level.

notes.front: An electrician in a boom-lift basket wants to clip his lanyard to the steel beam he is working on. What does section 1926.453 require?
notes.back: D: attach the lanyard to the boom or basket.
notes.choices:
A) Clip to the beam
B) No tie-off is needed in a basket
C) Stand on the basket rail to reach
D) Attach the lanyard to the boom or basket
notes.choicesExplained: A: belting off to an adjacent structure is not permitted. B: a lanyard is required. C: employees must stand firmly on the basket floor.
notes.explanation: Employees must also stand firmly on the basket floor rather than on its edge.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.453(b)(2)(iii), p. 270
notes.evidence: Belting off to an adjacent pole, structure, or equipment while working from an aerial lift shall not be permitted.

notes.front: A labourer is about to work on a scaffold for the first time. Which training does section 1926.454 require?
notes.back: D: training by a person qualified in the subject matter, on the hazards and how to control them.
notes.choices:
A) None, if a competent person inspects the scaffold
B) Training only for erectors
C) Reading the scaffold tag
D) Training by a person qualified in the subject matter, on the hazards and how to control them
notes.choicesExplained: A: inspection does not replace training. C is not training. B: users must be trained too; erectors need a competent person’s training.
notes.explanation: Section 1926.454 supplements the general training duty in section 1926.21(b)(2).
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.454(a), p. 271
notes.evidence: to recognize the hazards associated with the type of scaffold being used and to understand the procedures to control or minimize those hazards

notes.front: How does the toprail height for newer supported scaffolds differ from the Subpart M guardrail height?
notes.back: Scaffolds: 38 to 45 inches above the platform. Subpart M: 42 inches plus or minus 3, so 39 to 45.
notes.explanation: The ranges overlap but are not the same, so a 38-inch rail can pass on a scaffold and fail elsewhere.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.451(g)(4)(ii), p. 261
notes.evidence: The top edge height of toprails or equivalent member on supported scaffolds manufactured or placed in service after January 1, 2000 shall be installed between 38 inches (0.97 m) and 45 inches (1.2 m) above the platform surface.
